---
title: "Feign: Declarative HTTP Calls"
description: "A worked shop microservices lesson."

**Course source:** Day 2 §1. **Running system:** Product, Order and User services.

## Problem: URL construction leaks into business code

When Order needs Product, the first implementation constructs a URL, sends a request and parses the result. As APIs grow, every caller must repeat path construction, parameters, headers and error handling.

The supplied Spring course introduces **Feign**: a Java interface describes the remote operation, and the framework creates an HTTP client implementation. The business service can call a typed method without manually concatenating a URL.

~~~text
Order -> ProductClient.findById(7) -> HTTP GET /products/7
~~~

The interface is a *network contract*, not an ordinary in-process method call. It can time out, receive invalid data or fail because an instance has vanished.

## Equivalent small NestJS-style adapter

NestJS can make the boundary explicit by wrapping HTTP in a provider method:

~~~ts
import { Injectable } from '@nestjs/common';

@Injectable()
export class ProductClient {
  async findById(id: number) {
    const response = await fetch(
      'http://127.0.0.1:4101/products/' + id,
      { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(350) }
    );
    if (!response.ok) throw new Error('Product unavailable');
    return response.json();
  }
}
~~~

This illustrates *separating the remote client from the Order business logic*. It is an illustrative provider requiring a NestJS application, not a complete runnable file. The zero-dependency lab has the equivalent HTTP call.

## Feign and Ribbon in the course

The course's OpenFeign setup integrates with Ribbon and Eureka. Eureka resolves a logical service; Ribbon selects an instance; Feign expresses the HTTP operation. Those are **three different jobs**.

In newer Spring Cloud integrations, use current OpenFeign and load-balancer documentation instead of assuming Ribbon is present.

## Contract design

A good client has explicit request and response shapes, request deadlines, validation, errors and an ownership model for authentication headers. Hiding the URL construction must not hide the remote call's cost.

## Choose the right abstraction

Use a declarative client when many endpoints and consumers benefit from consistent typing and configuration. For one simple request, a small hand-written wrapper can remain clearer.

## Review questions

What failure does this technique address? Which state belongs to the caller and which belongs to the provider? What would you measure to confirm that it works?

## Mathematical Abstraction

The declarative method represents a fallible remote function.

$$
f_{\rm product}:\mathrm{ProductId}\rightarrow\mathrm{Result}(\mathrm{Product},\mathrm{RemoteError})
$$

The result type is a conceptual sum type: the call can return a product or an explicit failure, including timeout.
